evals.prompt: Our CTO came back from a conference convinced we need a Discord. We're Kestrel Metrics, an API observability tool, about 40 paying customers. Our support inbox gets maybe 6 tickets a month and honestly none of them repeat, they're all one-off integration questions. Our two biggest competitors both run Discords with thousands of members. There's an ecosystem Discord for the monitoring space where I know at least three of our users hang out already. Nobody on the team owns this - marketing said they'd keep an eye on it. Can you put together what channels we'd need and a rough launch plan?
evals.expected_output: A do-not-launch verdict with the five readiness gates scored and evidenced, a recommendation to participate in the existing ecosystem Discord instead, and an observable re-decision trigger. No channel list.
expectations: Returns a do-not-launch verdict rather than a launch plan
Scores all five readiness gates by name - demand, owner, purpose, venue vacuum, seed supply - with a pass, weak or fail mark on each
Marks the demand gate as failing and cites the 6 tickets a month with no repeats as the evidence
Marks the venue-vacuum gate as failing because the monitoring ecosystem Discord already hosts part of this audience
Marks the owner gate as failing and treats "marketing said they'd keep an eye on it" as an ownership gap rather than a staffing detail to settle later
States explicitly that competitors having a Discord is not accepted as evidence of demand
Notes that the 40 named customers are what the seed-supply gate has to work with, and that coverage rather than headcount is what it tests
Recommends participating in the existing ecosystem Discord instead of opening a new venue
Produces no channel list or category tree for a new Discord
Names an observable re-decision trigger such as a repeat-question volume or users starting to answer each other, rather than a date to revisit
States the verdict rule applied: three or fewer gates passing means do not launch

evals.prompt: Orbwright makes a distributed task queue library, commercial license, roughly 900 paying teams. We've already signed up for Slack and I've got the workspace created. Context: we get 20-30 configuration questions a month by email, about a third are duplicates, and four of our users regularly answer each other in our GitHub issues. Dario owns this with 6 hours a week protected indefinitely, but he batches it - he's heads-down on the engine most of the week and can realistically look at it two or three afternoons. The answers we give stay correct for a year or more since the config surface barely changes, and honestly a big reason we want this is that people google our error strings and land nowhere right now. We have 60 users we could invite by name across four topic areas and three continents. Help us plan the launch.
evals.expected_output: A launch verdict, Slack treated as a hypothesis and the owned real-time chat class deleted with reopen triggers recorded, an owned async forum recommended with the class named before any vendor, and the vendor figures flagged for re-verification.
expectations: Treats the already-chosen Slack as a hypothesis and runs the readiness gates before discussing the platform
Scores all five gates and returns a launch verdict
Deletes owned real-time chat as a venue class rather than demoting it in a ranking
Gives at least two distinct reasons real-time chat is deleted here: its archive is not indexed, and the owner cannot be present most days
Records a reopen trigger for the deleted real-time chat class on the venue line of the brief
Recommends an owned async forum as the surviving venue class
Names the venue class before naming any vendor
States the venue ranking out loud rather than leaving it implied by the order things are listed in
Notes that Slack's free plan retains only 90 days of message history, which removes the searchable archive the error-string search goal depends on
Notes that per-seat pricing makes an open community structurally more expensive as it grows, unlike per-instance forum pricing
Flags that vendor pricing, retention and export claims must be re-verified on the vendor's own page before the recommendation is final
Does not recommend running Slack and a forum as two primary venues at once

evals.prompt: I'm the founder at Fernbrook, we make a schema-migration CLI, about 2,400 weekly active installs and 150 paying teams. I want to open a community and I want it to do three things: take support load off me, give us a steady stream of roadmap input from the people who actually run migrations in production, and build up a group of vocal users who bring us signups. Demand is there - I get the same four questions constantly by DM and two users already answer each other in our issues. I can give it 8 hours a week, no question, and I've got 45 people I could invite tomorrow. Nobody else serves this niche. Let's get going - what platform and what does week one look like?
evals.expected_output: The three goals mapped to SPACES letters, the purpose gate held open until exactly one primary is chosen, the primary converted into a measurable claim, and no venue or channel structure proposed before that.
expectations: Names the outcomes using the SPACES vocabulary and maps each of the three stated goals to its letter: Support, Product, and Acquisition and advocacy
Refuses to accept all three as co-primary and requires exactly one primary outcome
Marks the purpose gate as not passing while the three outcomes remain unranked
States that the primary outcome decides the community model, the venue class and the thresholds
Attributes the one-objective rule to CMX's SPACES model rather than presenting it as the assistant's own preference
Allows secondary outcomes but requires them stated explicitly and ranked below the primary
Converts the chosen primary into a measurable claim carrying a number and a timeframe, not a restatement of the goal
Does not propose a venue, platform or channel structure before the primary outcome is settled
Asks the user to pick the primary rather than silently choosing one for them

Notes that if acquisition and advocacy becomes the primary, none of the four named community models (support-driven, product-development, education and enablement, founder-led) applies and the shape has to be designed from the outcome instead

evals.prompt: Quillstack, we build a feature-flag SDK. Getting ready to open a user forum. Where we stand: 40+ repeat setup questions came in last quarter, a dozen of them duplicates, and users answer each other in our repo already. Priya owns it, 7 hours a week signed off by her manager through next year and beyond. Primary goal is support deflection, we've written it as cutting duplicate setup tickets by half in two quarters. No existing space covers us. On invitees I've got 24 people I can name, though realistically only one of them besides Priya is someone I'd trust to actually answer things, and they're all in Central Europe while about 60% of our installs are in North America and APAC. Marketing wants to lock 4 November for the announcement so they can slot it into the quarterly push. Can you confirm the date and write up the plan?
evals.expected_output: A launch-on-a-delayed-date verdict with seed supply as the weak gate, a written mitigation the date is gated on instead of the calendar, and the opening sequence gated on observed activity.
expectations: Returns a launch-on-a-delayed-date verdict rather than confirming 4 November
Gates the launch on the mitigation landing rather than on a calendar date
Writes the mitigation down as a specific named action, such as recruiting a second reliable answerer and adding time-zone coverage
Marks seed supply as the weak gate and the other four as passing
States that coverage - one reliable answerer per topic area, and at least two time zones for a global audience - is what the seed-supply gate tests, not headcount
Does not treat 24 named invitees as an automatic pass merely because it clears 20
Applies the verdict rule for four gates passing with a written mitigation
Requires founding members who already behave like contributors or advocates rather than passive newcomers
Does not recommend padding the invite list with additional names to hit a number
Keeps the opening sequence - founding cohort, invited beta, public announcement - gated on observed activity rather than on the fixed November date

evals.prompt: Arcmesh here. We opened a Discourse forum for our infrastructure-as-code tool 90 days ago and I need to decide what to do next. We announced it during our keynote at a big conference in month one and got a huge rush - we're at 6,200 members now. Month one was incredible, months two and three feel much flatter but I'm told that's normal. Current numbers: 61% of questions get an answer within 24 hours, 28% of posts are written by someone who isn't on our team, 55% of threads have at least one reply, and our five most active members account for 74% of all engagement. Marketing has budget left and wants to run a paid campaign to push us to 15,000 members this quarter, arguing that more people means more conversation. Thoughts on the plan?
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the promotion plan with the reason, every failing signal named against its threshold, the conference month rejected as a comparison baseline, and the fold-back path offered in order with a named decision owner.
expectations: Rejects more promotion or paid acquisition as the response, and gives the reason: more joins into a silent room lowers every ratio
Names each day-90 signal that sits below its pass threshold, alongside the threshold it missed

Identifies at least four failing signals against the baseline thresholds of over 90% answered within 24 hours, over 50% non-staff posts, over 80% of threads with a reply, and under 50% engagement concentration in the top five members
States that the 6,200 member count is a joins counter rather than a health signal
Warns against measuring against the conference-driven launch month and requires a trailing baseline instead
Names burstiness - the spike-and-decay pattern releases, conferences and media coverage produce - as the reason the launch month is not a valid comparison
Flags the 74% top-five engagement concentration as fragility: those five leaving takes the community with them
Offers the fold-back path and states its options in order: archive read-only, then merge into the space the audience already uses, then convert to a plain support channel
Explains that archiving preserves the answers and their search traffic at near-zero standing effort
Recommends re-running the shape and seeding work against the specific failing signals rather than a general effort increase
Names a decision owner for the fold-back call
Does not propose adding more channels or categories to lift activity

evals.prompt: Vireo Labs. We've had a Slack for our platform users for about 14 months, 1,100 members. It was lively for the first half year and now it's pretty much dead - a few messages a week, mostly us. Leadership is calling it a failed experiment. I want to relaunch it properly: figure out which numbers we should actually be watching, work out whether it's genuinely dying or just seasonal, and come back with something defensible. Where do we start?
evals.expected_output: A routing call to the community-health skill in owner/repo@skill form, with the reason, and a stop - no gates scored, no venue recommendation, no seeding plan.
expectations: Routes the request to the community-health skill instead of running the launch workflow
States that this skill does not apply to a community that already exists
Stops after the routing call rather than half-running the readiness gates
Produces no launch brief, venue recommendation or founding-cohort plan
Names the target as samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-community-health, in owner/repo@skill form
Distinguishes the one case that would keep the work here: deciding whether to shut the community down
Does not read "relaunch" as a request to pick a new platform
Gives the reason for routing: half-running the workflow on the wrong problem wastes the user's time

evals.prompt: Palebright, we ship an embedded database. We're two weeks from opening a GitHub Discussions space for our users and my VP wants targets written down before we go. What she's proposed: 2,000 members by day 90, and getting the share of members who never post below 40% - she's seen our beta group where about four in five people just read and thinks that's the main thing to fix. She also wants me to just check in at the end of the quarter and see how it went. Can you turn that into a measurement plan?
evals.expected_output: Both proposed targets rejected with published anchors, replaced by active-member counts and the six day-90 ratio signals labelled by basis, a 48-hour-window response commitment, and day-30 leading indicators.
expectations: Rejects the "below 40% lurkers" target and states that around 90% of members never posting is the baseline condition, not a launch defect
Attributes the 90-9-1 participation-inequality finding to Jakob Nielsen at NN/g rather than presenting it as an unsourced rule of thumb
Notes that the beta group's four-in-five read-only share is at or better than that baseline rather than a problem to fix
Rejects the 2,000-member target as a joins counter rather than a health signal
Sets targets on the number of active members and on ratio signals instead

Proposes day-90 pass thresholds covering at least: answered within 24 hours, non-staff share of posts, new members posting within 7 days, monthly active share, threads with at least one reply, and top-five engagement concentration
Labels which thresholds are published findings and which are baselines offered as a starting hypothesis to recalibrate
Requires the thresholds be written down before launch rather than assessed afterwards, and says why
Recommends publishing a response-time commitment and places it inside a 48-hour window
Cites the 48-hour responsiveness evidence as a published finding rather than an invented target

evals.prompt: Northkeep sells a data-pipeline platform to enterprises - 55 customers, contracts between $40k and $300k a year. The people who'd actually use a community are data engineers at those accounts; the people who sign the renewal are VPs of Data who I'm certain would never post anything. A good chunk of our users are at banks and insurers whose security policy flat-out bans pasting code or architecture into anything public. Three of our largest accounts have separately asked us for a dedicated private channel just for their team. Demand is solid - we get the same eight or nine pipeline-tuning questions from different accounts every month, and two customers have swapped notes on a call. Marcus owns it, 10 hours a week. We can name 30 invitees. What should we build?
evals.expected_output: A B2B plan: buyer/user split with a separate buyer signal path, public venue classes deleted with reopen triggers, the private-channel requests refused as community and gated as support, and percentage thresholds adjusted with stated reasoning.
expectations: Names the buyer and user split explicitly: the room fills with data engineers while renewal depends on VPs of Data who never post
Requires a separate signal path to the buyer rather than assuming community activity reaches them
Deletes the rented public space and forge-native discussions as venue classes, because both are public by construction and the bank and insurer users cannot post publicly
Treats those as deletions rather than demotions, and records the trigger that would reopen each
Does not grant the three requested private per-customer channels as a community feature
States that private per-customer channels fragment the community and drift into support contracts
Gates any per-customer channel on contract value and staffs it as support rather than as community
Adjusts the day-90 percentage thresholds for a deliberately small, high-value room and proposes absolute counts alongside them
States the reasoning for that threshold adjustment in the brief instead of silently changing the numbers
Expects weekday business-hours activity rather than evenings and weekends
Raises data residency, privacy or moderation obligations as a constraint to check before committing to a venue
Recommends exactly one primary venue

evals.prompt: Saltmarsh - we make an open-source workflow engine, and the community decision is already made and signed off, all the readiness boxes are ticked. Here's where the plan stands and I'd like you to sharpen it. Launch day is 3 March: we send to our newsletter, 12,000 subscribers, all at once. I've got 11 channels prepped and named: general, announcements, help, showcase, jobs, random, kubernetes, python, go, contributors, off-topic. And I've sent 40 people a message saying "hey, we're opening a community, come join!" Anything obviously missing?
evals.expected_output: The day-one blast replaced by a three-stage sequence gated on observed activity, the channel tree cut to a small surface, the invitation rewritten as a time-boxed personal ask, 5-10 seeded posts shipped with their answers, a ritual from week one, and a published response-time commitment.
expectations: Rejects announcing to the 12,000-subscriber newsletter on day one and gives the reason: it spends the single first impression on an empty room
Replaces the day-one announcement with a three-stage sequence: founding cohort, then invited beta, then public announcement
Gates each transition between stages on observed activity rather than on a calendar date
Cuts the 11 planned channels down to a small opening surface
States that every empty room signals a dead community, and that rooms get added only when an existing one gets noisy
Rewrites the "come join" invitation into a personal ask naming why that specific person and what is being asked of them
Time-boxes the founding-member commitment, for example to the first quarter, rather than leaving it open-ended
Specifies seeding roughly 5-10 posts that model the behaviour wanted
Requires the seeded questions to ship with their answers, and gives the reason: an unanswered seeded question teaches newcomers that questions go unanswered here
Installs one recurring ritual from week one
Publishes a response-time commitment and treats unanswered posts as the primary launch defect
Targets the member mix rather than the headcount, requiring contributors and advocates in the founding cohort rather than passive newcomers
Checks coverage across the 40 invitees - a reliable answerer per topic area and time-zone spread - rather than accepting the count

evals.prompt: Duneshift is pre-1.0 developer infrastructure - a runtime for edge functions. We have about 30 design partners and the single thing we need from a community is tight, fast product feedback: we ship breaking changes most weeks and we want to hear within hours when something lands badly. Ines, our founder, is genuinely in the room all day, and we have a named support rota of three people covering Berlin, São Paulo and Singapore so someone is awake basically all the time. Our answers go stale within a few weeks anyway because the API keeps moving, and we have zero interest in search traffic - we're not even indexed yet and don't want to be. All 30 partners are on GitHub and we have a public repo. What venue should we open?
evals.expected_output: Owned real-time chat recommended as a deliberate promotion against the efficiency order, with the ranking stated on multiple axes, the two promotion conditions named, the lost archive accepted explicitly, and the class named before any vendor.
expectations: Recommends owned real-time chat as the venue class
States the venue-class ranking out loud on more than one axis - efficiency, effort, value, compliance cost - rather than a single blended order
Acknowledges that real-time chat sits last on the efficiency ratio and is being promoted here anyway
Names the two conditions justifying the promotion: the primary outcome is Product (or Engagement), and continuous presence is genuinely staffed by named people
Cites the named three-person rota across Berlin, São Paulo and Singapore as the staffing evidence behind the promotion
States that the unindexed archive is an acceptable loss here because the answers go stale within weeks and search traffic is not wanted
Does not justify the choice with "that's where developers are" or with ambition
Notes that real-time chat carries the highest standing-presence cost and the highest compliance cost of the four classes
Names the venue class before naming any vendor
Maps the design-partner feedback goal to the SPACES letter for Product
Recommends one primary venue, giving any second surface a distinct, non-overlapping job

evals.prompt: Tenvale, we do a static-analysis tool for Rust. I ran the numbers and I don't think we're ready for a community but I still need to bring something back to the exec team. Situation: support volume is 5 tickets a month and nothing repeats, and I've never once seen a user answer another user anywhere. The Rust ecosystem Discord has an active channel that covers our problem space and a handful of our users post there. What we actually want out of this is product direction - concretely, about 10 usable roadmap signals a month. Nils owns it with 4 hours a week and we can name 35 users we'd invite. Budget is basically zero, so give me the cheapest thing we can do instead and I'll sell that.
evals.expected_output: A do-not-launch verdict, the cheapest option explicitly refused in favour of the alternative returning the most evidence per standing hour, the ordering stated out loud, the feedback loop ruled out despite the Product outcome, and an observable re-decision trigger.
expectations: Returns a do-not-launch verdict on three of five gates passing
Explicitly refuses to pick the cheapest option and states the selection rule: the alternative returning the most evidence per hour of standing presence
States the ordering of the alternatives out loud rather than presenting an unranked list
Recommends answering publicly where the audience already is, meaning the Rust ecosystem Discord channel, as the primary alternative
Explains that answering publicly tests the demand gate and the venue-vacuum gate at the same time
Rules out the email or issue-based feedback loop despite the Product outcome, because it is one-to-one by construction and structurally cannot produce peer-conversation evidence
Notes that a troubleshooting or FAQ surface is the cheapest standing commitment but barely moves the demand gate
Does not promote scheduled office hours here, since seed supply is not the failing gate
Emits no compliance-cost axis for these alternatives, or states that none of the five makes the team the host of a space
Names an observable re-decision trigger, such as a repeat-question volume or users starting to answer each other, rather than a review date
States what evidence each recommended alternative is expected to produce toward the blocked launch decision
